In brief

For the voyeuristic scene in Nausicaa, from Gerty MacDowell's introduction to her departure, Joyce borrowed extensively from an earlier depiction of one of his own romantic reveries. At the end of part 4 of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man Stephen walks away from the church (quite literally) and finds himself gazing rapturously at a girl wading on the beach, her skirts pulled up high around her waist to free her legs. This seaside erotic vision confirms him in his choice to be an artist and cherish earthly beauty. The action is repeated when a young woman exposes her underwear to Bloom, and the lush language of the scene in A Portrait, nearly sexual but not quite in Stephen's distinctive way, gets recycled too. Dozens of similar words and phrases in Nausicaa praise Gerty's delicate female beauty and suggest that human love can feel a lot like religious worship.

At more length

The girl in A Portrait is lovingly compared to a bird:

Her long slender bare legs were delicate as a crane's and pure save where an emerald trail of seaweed had fashioned itself as a sign upon the flesh. Her thighs, fuller and softhued as ivory, were bared almost to the hips where the white fringes of her drawers were like featherings of soft white down. Her slateblue skirts were kilted boldly about her waist and dovetailed behind her. Her bosom was as a bird's soft and slight, slight and soft as the breast of some darkplumaged dove. But her long fair hair was girlish, and touched with the wonder of mortal beauty, her face.
    She was alone and still, gazing out to sea; and when she felt his presence and the worship of his eyes her eyes turned to him in quiet sufferance of his gaze, without shame or wantonness. Long, long she suffered his gaze and then quietly withdrew her eyes from his [...] and a faint flame trembled on her cheek.

Avian images have mostly disappeared from the catalogue of Gerty's charms, but the rest of the picture remains. Pronounced "beautiful by all who knew her," seen lovely "in her sweet girlish shyness," he has a "softly featured face," arms that are "white and soft," a "soft body," and a face "almost spiritual in its ivorylike purity." Her words are "more musical than the cooing of the ringdove." Her eyes are "the bluest Irish blue," and blue appears also in her blouse, the brim and bow of her hat, the ribbons of her underwear, and her garters. She has "delicate hands," "snowy slender arms," and exquisite long hair. She leans back to let Bloom see "all her graceful beautifully shaped legs like that, supply soft and delicately rounded." The focus on the clothes clutched about the bird-girl's waist returns in Gerty's memory of the time when Reggy Wylie "stole an arm round her waist" and "she went white to the very lips."

Joyce also allows Gerty to make Cissy Caffrey into a poor parody of the crane-like girl, a shoddy imitation: "She ran with long gandery strides it was a wonder she didn't rip up her skirt at the side that was too tight on her because there was a lot of the tomboy about Cissy Caffrey and she was a forward piece whenever she thought she had a good opportunity to show and just because she was a good runner she ran like that so that he could see all the end of her petticoat running and her skinny shanks up as far as possible. It would have served her just right if she had tripped up over something accidentally on purpose with her high crooked French heels on her to make her look tall and got a fine tumble. Tableau! That would have been a very charming expose for a gentleman like that to witness." Bloom's good fortune in seeing Gerty's underwear is here introduced comically as a thought that he might see Cissy's.

Both scenes consist mostly of looking. Like the girl "gazing out to sea," Gerty sits on the strand "gazing far away into the distance." The girl quietly suffers Stephen's gaze "without shame or wantonness," and Gerty feels the same absence of sexual impropriety: "she wasn't ashamed and he wasn't either to look in that immodest way." The girl does, however, recognize the nature of the gaze and "a faint flame trembled on her cheek." Gerty blushes three times, the first two in response to indelicate things her female companions say and the third in response to Bloom's erotic gaze: "She felt the warm flush, a danger signal always with Gerty MacDowell, surging and flaming into her cheeks.” The "Long, long" interval in which the girl locks eyes with Stephen returns in Gerty's dream of an older man who will "comfort her with a long long kiss."

Also carried over from one text to the other are details suggestive of sexual choice and sexual passion. In the excitement of being saved from a regimented and puritanical existence Stephen thinks repeatedly of "wild" life, wild air, wild joy. Gerty feels "wild, untrammeled, free" in her discovery of a new love. Stephen experiences, in the chastely quiet manner of one newly freed from the seminary, a muffled ejaculation: "—Heavenly God! cried Stephen's soul, in an outburst of profane joy." Gerty too mutes a palpably sexual cry: "She would fain have cried to him chokingly, held out her snowy slender arms to him to come, to feel his lips laid on her white brow, the cry of a young girl's love." Walking away from the vision, Stephen's "cheeks were aflame; his body was aglow; his limbs were trembling." Gerty, leaning far back for Bloom's benefit, finds herself "trembling in every limb."

In the aftermath of his powerfully erotic response to the girl Stephen feels that he has received an anticlerical vocation: "Her eyes had called to him and his soul had leaped at the call." Gerty calls more actively and Bloom responds more carnally. After their shared, but dissimilar, climaxes, the narrative mimics a chaste young woman chiding a lewd old man: "Leopold Bloom (for it is he) stands silent, with bowed head before those young guileless eyes. What a brute he had been! At it again? A fair unsullied soul had called to him and, wretch that he was, how had he answered? An utter cad he had been!"

Most striking of all the intertextual echoes are suggestions that sexual adoration resembles religious devotion. Like the girl on the beach, Gerty is clad in blue and white—the iconographic colors of Mary. She is a "radiant little vision" resembling the "pure radiance" of the Blessed Virgin—a word that recalls Stephen's Aquinian aesthetics in A Portrait. His adored virgin chastely accepts "the worship of his eyes," and Gerty does the same with Bloom: "His dark eyes fixed themselves on her again drinking in her every contour, literally worshipping at her shrine." (The worship is very much metaphorical, not literal.) Religious language briefly wars with sexual awareness when Gerty thinks that Bloom "couldn't resist the sight of the wondrous revealment half offered like those skirtdancers behaving so immodest before gentlemen looking and he kept on looking, looking." The pornographic analogue destroys her pretense of Marian purity: the wondrous revelation is her vagina, only half offered because it is veiled in white underwear, "the fabric that caresses the skin," and because Gerty is not quite ready to offer up her body to intercourse with a total stranger.

Analogizing this lewd interaction to the devotional worship taking place in the Star of the Sea church is daring, provocative, offensive. Joyce was not yet ready for that in A Portrait but he may have had it in the back of his mind, because he adumbrated what he would do later with Stephen's "outburst of profane joy." Fritz Senn observes in a chapter on Nausicaa that the etymology of "profane" is "outside the temple" (Critical Essays 286). That is exactly where Gerty sits half-offering her genitals to Bloom while the men inside the Star of the Sea church praise the generosity of God's mother, and Nausicaa invites readers to look back to the earlier novel by calling the church "that simple fane beside the waves."

Senn notes many of the parallels with A Portrait and adds some others from a different source. When Joyce fell in lust with Marthe Fleischmann in Zurich, he wrote several letters to her, as well as a postcard, now lost, addressed from "Odysseus" to "Nausicaa." The letters contain several phrases that he would later adapt to Gerty's beauty. Where Joyce confesses to "une espèce de fascination," Bloom is "fascinated by a loveliness that made him gaze." Joyce describes Martha's face as pale, tired, and sad ("Dein gesight, aber so blass, so müde und so traurig!"), and Gerty has "sad downcast eyes," a "tired feeling," and a "waxen pallor" to her face. Joyce imagines Martha's kisses falling over his heart "weich wie Rosenblätter, sanft wie Tau" (soft as rose leaves, soft as dew). In Gerty's eyes the fireworks falling over Sandymount are "all greeny dewy stars falling with golden, O so lovely! O, so soft, sweet, soft!"

The Zurich letters also inform some of Gerty's thoughts about Bloom. She wonders whether "he had suffered," recalling Joyce's response to an illness of Martha's: "moi, j'ai souffert aussi." Joyce presents himself as a "pauvre chercheur dans ce monde" who has "vécu et péché et créé"—a poor searcher in this world who has lived and sinned and created. Bloom's eyes fix on Gerty "as though they would search her through and through, read her very soul," and she supposes that he "had erred and sinned and wandered." Finally, Joyce notes that Martha has given him a sign ("vous m'avez fait un signe"), like the handkerchief that Gerty waves for Bloom's benefit just before leaving.

The vertiginous juxtapositions of tone in Nausicaa pose real challenges for readers. After several dozen similar irruptions in Cyclops, the saccharine imitation of hackneyed female speech in the first half of the chapter feels like a mocking parody, and the return of Bloom's skeptically judging voice in the second half feels like the puncturing of a romantic balloon. But a third major stylistic component of the chapter complicates this contrast. Joyce includes in the first section an emotional register—powerfully sexual, delicately poetic, spiritually reverent—that he had already explored in propria persona. This language crosses the chapter's seemingly stark division of male and female sensibilities, establishing a vital middle ground between Gerty's jejune fancies and Bloom's jaded inquisitions. By dissolving that barrier it helps create the impression that something meaningful has happened between the two people.

Mockery usually keeps company with jocoserious appreciation in Joyce's writing, and Nausicaa weights that balance in a most interesting way. If it seems odd that Joyce would subject his own private and cherished sexual impulses to raucous guffaws in the way that he does here, readers may recall the way he balances romantic affirmations with withering ironies in A Portrait of the Artist.

John Hunt 2026

title: Worshipping at her shrine
